title: Effects of visualizing uncertainty on decision-making in a target identification scenario
research_question: How does explicitly visualizing uncertainty in spatio-temporal sensor information affect expert target-identification and prioritization decisions under time pressure?
methodology: The study uses a prototype for interactive analysis of multivariate spatio-temporal sensor data in an air-defense-style target-identification scenario. Uncertainty is encoded through graphical features including line thickness, semi-transparent positional circles, and a track-quality value. Twenty-two experienced air-traffic operators are divided into groups with and without uncertainty visualization and perform identification and prioritization tasks under high time pressure and cognitive load. Outcomes include decision attempts, selected identity and priority, workload, time, classification performance, and expressed confidence.

key_findings.finding: Participants shown uncertainty information required significantly fewer attempts before making their final target identification.
The uncertainty-visualization group assigned significantly higher priority values and chose more hostile or suspect target identities.
Displaying uncertainty did not significantly increase expressed workload or average decision time.
Uncertainty visualization did not produce a significant improvement in classification performance measured through true positives, false negatives, and false positives.
Participants' expressed confidence was not significantly changed by the uncertainty visualization.
The authors interpret the more conservative identity and priority assignments as possible evidence that experts adopt a worst-case stance when uncertainty is visible in a safety-critical setting.

limitations: Only 22 participants were studied, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The participants were experienced air-traffic operators working in an air-defense-style experimental scenario rather than necessarily operators performing their normal operational task.
The experiment concerns one safety-critical identification domain and does not establish that the same behavioral response occurs in workplace briefing or task prioritization.
The accessible abstract does not expose detailed randomization procedures, exact effect sizes, statistical tests, or experimental materials.
The study evaluates uncertainty presentation at a decision point rather than longitudinal state tracking, adaptation over repeated cycles, or omission and repetition.
raw_claims: The experiment studies decision making when uncertain sensor information must be interpreted quickly.
One experimental condition explicitly visualized uncertainty and the comparison condition did not.
Uncertainty was represented through visual properties of sensor values and target position as well as a track-quality indicator.
The uncertainty group reached final identifications in fewer attempts.
Visible uncertainty changed the identities and priorities assigned to targets.
The uncertainty group tended toward higher priorities and more hostile or suspect classifications.
Uncertainty presentation did not significantly increase workload.
Uncertainty presentation did not significantly increase average decision time.
Objective classification performance and expressed confidence did not significantly improve.
